🐛 Describe the bug
When attempting to create a custom operator in C++ (following this PyTorch tutorial) I ran into an issue with the find_package(Torch REQURED) call in my CMakeLists.txt. The operator I was attempting to create utilized code from the torch/csrc/utils/tensor_numpy.h header file and when I would try to compile the operator, I'd get the following error:
Undefined symbols for architecture arm64:
  "torch::utils::tensor_to_numpy(at::Tensor const&, bool)", referenced from:
      numpy_test(at::Tensor) in test_opp.cpp.o
ld: symbol(s) not found for architecture arm64

Below is my C++ code for the operator and my CMakeLists.txt:
test_opp.cpp
#include <torch/script.h>
#include <torch/csrc/utils/tensor_numpy.h>

using namespace torch::utils;


torch::Tensor numpy_test(torch::Tensor tensor) {

  PyObject* array = tensor_to_numpy(tensor);

  return tensor;
}

TORCH_LIBRARY(test_ops, m) {
  m.def("numpy_test", numpy_test);
}
CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22.2 FATAL_ERROR)
project(numpy_test)

find_package(Python COMPONENTS Interpreter Development)
find_package(Torch REQUIRED)

add_library(numpy_test SHARED test_opp.cpp)
target_compile_features(numpy_test PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
target_link_libraries(
        numpy_test
        PUBLIC "${TORCH_LIBRARIES}"
        PUBLIC Python::Python
)
The operator was very basic -- really just testing out the process of creating a custom one and getting familiar with how that all works.
I was able to resolve my issue by updating the CMakeLists.txt file to the following:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22.2 FATAL_ERROR)
project(numpy_test)

find_package(Python COMPONENTS Interpreter Development)
find_package(Torch REQUIRED)

file(
        GLOB
        LIBTORCH_PYTHON
        "$ENV{VIRTUAL_ENV}/lib/python3.9/site-packages/torch/lib/libtorch_python.dylib"
)

add_library(numpy_test SHARED test_opp.cpp)
target_compile_features(numpy_test PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
target_link_libraries(
        numpy_test
        PUBLIC "${TORCH_LIBRARIES}"
        PUBLIC ${LIBTORCH_PYTHON}
        PUBLIC Python::Python
)
Pretty much just directly adding the libtorch_python.dylib library to my target. This change allowed my operator to be complied without any issues.
Not entirely sure if this is a bug with the find_package(Torch ...) call or if there is another official way to add these dynamic libraries in CMake.

🐛 Describe the bug
Hi @drisspg, after more hours of debugging than I am comfortable to admit, I noticed the following breaking change between PyTorch 2.0.1 and PyTorch 2.1.
The issue can be reproduced both with torch-2.1.0+cu118 & 2.2.0.dev20231030+cu118. There is no issue on 2.0.1
For fp32 inputs to SDPA on CUDA device & passing a custom attn_mask, we have the following:

PyTorch 2.0.1: dispatches to math (RuntimeError: No available kernel. Aborting execution. for other backends)
PyTorch 2.1: dispatches to mem-efficient attention (likely following #96099). And it appears that the mem-efficient attention backend outputs wrong results when passing non-contigous key/value, while the math backend goes just fine.

Reproduction:
import torch
import copy

num_heads = 16
head_dim = 128
torch.set_printoptions(threshold=1000000, sci_mode=True)

def _attn_sdpa(query, key, value, attention_mask=None, contiguify=False, enable_mem_efficient=False):
    query_shape = query.shape
    batch_size = query_shape[0]
    kv_seq_len = key.shape[-2]

    query_length = query_shape[1]

    # NOTE: Maybe there is better than this?
    query = query.view(batch_size, query_length, num_heads, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)

    # Without these unsqueeze, SDPA complains as the query and key/value have a different number of dimensions.
    key = key.unsqueeze(1)
    value = value.unsqueeze(1)

    # Although these expand are not numerically useful, PyTorch 2.1 can not dispatch to mem-efficient attention
    # and flash attention (No available kernel.  Aborting execution.) from the shapes
    # query = [batch_size, num_heads, query_length, head_dim]
    # key = [batch_size, 1, kv_length, head_dim]
    # value = [batch_size, 1, kv_length, head_dim]
    # which is unfortunate. Hopefully can be improved in the future. These expand should not be too expansive as they do not do memory copy.

    value = value.expand(-1, num_heads, -1, -1)

        value = value.contiguous()

    print("value contiguous", value.is_contiguous())

    else:

            query,
            key,
            value,
            attn_mask=attention_mask,
            dropout_p=0.0,
            is_causal=False,
        )

    return sdpa_result

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Currently when cudagraphing the optimizer in isolation, it's possible that the grads are not from an upstream cudagraph. The solution in this case is to mark the grads as static using the mark_static_address API.   Inductor will generate a copy for each grad in this case, catastrophically impacting perf, so we should print a warning in this case.

🐛 Describe the bug
When we ignore modules with any trainable parameters in FSDP, an error occurs when we try to continue training after loading a distributed checkpoint for the optimizer.
Key works: FSDP, ignore modules, distributed checkpoint, loading optimizer states.
The following script is from PyTorch checkpoint example (I added some code to allow ignoring one of the linear layer): https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b97afc401843aae2b07dffca8f00d212ba1d470e/torch/distributed/checkpoint/examples/fsdp_checkpoint_example.py. The original script works well on my end. But when I added some code to allow ignoring one of the linear layer, it raises an error.
I've confirmed that it works correctly if no modules are ignored or when using a full-state checkpoint. The model itself loads correctly, but the loaded optimizer state encounters issues. The loading process itself doesn't raise any errors, but an error arises at the optimizer.step() stage.
import os
import shutil

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dist_cp
import torch.multiprocessing as mp

from torch.distributed.fsdp import FullyShardedDataParallel as FSDP
from torch.distributed.fsdp.fully_sharded_data_parallel import StateDictType
from torch.distributed.checkpoint.optimizer import (
    load_sharded_optimizer_state_dict,
)

CHECKPOINT_DIR = "scratch/checkpoint/py"

class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(Net, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(8, 8, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(8, 8, bias=False)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(8, 8, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.fc1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = self.fc2(x)
        x = self.fc3(x)
        output = F.log_softmax(x, dim=1)
        return output


def opt_at(opt, idx):
    return list(opt.state.values())[idx]


def init_model(dry_run=True):
    model = Net()
    model = FSDP(model.cuda(dist.get_rank()), ignored_modules=[model.fc1])
    optim = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
    if dry_run:
        optim.zero_grad()
        model(torch.rand(8, 8)).sum().backward()
        optim.step()
    return model, optim


def train(model, optim):
    for _ in range(10):
        optim.zero_grad()
        model(torch.rand(8, 8)).sum().backward()
        optim.step()


def print_params(stage, model_1, model_2, optim_1, optim_2):
    # with FSDP.summon_full_params(model_1):
    #     with FSDP.summon_full_params(model_2):
    #         print(
    #             f"{stage} --- rank: {dist.get_rank()}\n"
    #             f"model.weight: {model_1.weight}\n"
    #             f"model_2.weight:{model_2.weight}\n"
    #             f"model.bias: {model_1.bias}\n"
    #             f"model_2.bias: {model_2.bias}\n"
    #         )

    # print(
    #     f"{stage} --- rank: {dist.get_rank()}\n"
    #     f"optim exp_avg:{opt_at(optim_1, 0)['exp_avg']}\n"
    #     f"optim_2 exp_avg:{opt_at(optim_2, 0)['exp_avg']}\n"
    #     f"optim exp_avg_sq:{opt_at(optim_1, 0)['exp_avg_sq']}\n"
    #     f"optim_2 exp_avg_sq:{opt_at(optim_2, 0)['exp_avg_sq']}\n"
    # )
    pass


def run_fsdp_checkpoint_example(rank, world_size):
    # Set up world pg
    os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "localhost"
    os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = "12355"

    # Initialize the process group
    dist.init_process_group("cpu:gloo,cuda:nccl", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)
    torch.cuda.set_device(rank)

    # Create a model
    model_1, optim_1 = init_model()

    # Save the model to CHECKPOINT_DIR
    with FSDP.state_dict_type(model_1, StateDictType.SHARDED_STATE_DICT):
        state_dict = {
            "model": model_1.state_dict(),
            "optim": FSDP.optim_state_dict(model_1, optim_1),
        }

        dist_cp.save_state_dict(
            state_dict=state_dict,
            storage_writer=dist_cp.FileSystemWriter(CHECKPOINT_DIR),
        )

    # Create a second model
    model_2, optim_2 = init_model()

    # Print the model parameters for both models.
    # Before loading, the parameters should be different.
    print_params("Before loading", model_1, model_2, optim_1, optim_2)

    # Load model_2 with parameters saved in CHECKPOINT_DIR
    with FSDP.state_dict_type(model_2, StateDictType.SHARDED_STATE_DICT):
        state_dict = {
            "model": model_2.state_dict(),
            # cannot load the optimizer state_dict together with the model state_dict
        }

        dist_cp.load_state_dict(
            state_dict=state_dict,
            storage_reader=dist_cp.FileSystemReader(CHECKPOINT_DIR),
        )
        model_2.load_state_dict(state_dict["model"])

        optim_state = load_sharded_optimizer_state_dict(
            model_state_dict=state_dict["model"],
            optimizer_key="optim",
            storage_reader=dist_cp.FileSystemReader(CHECKPOINT_DIR),
        )

        flattened_osd = FSDP.optim_state_dict_to_load(
            model_2, optim_2, optim_state["optim"]
        )
        optim_2.load_state_dict(flattened_osd)

    # Print the model parameters for both models.
    # After loading, the parameters should be the same.
    print_params("After loading", model_1, model_2, optim_1, optim_2)

    train(model_2, optim_2)

    # Shut down world pg
    dist.destroy_process_group()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    world_size = torch.cuda.device_count()
    print(f"Running fsdp checkpoint example on {world_size} devices.")
    shutil.rmtree(CHECKPOINT_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
    mp.spawn(
        run_fsdp_checkpoint_example,
        args=(world_size,),
        nprocs=world_size,
        join=True,
    )

🐛 Describe the bug
After exporting a NanoGPT torch model to ONNX, the outputs remain constant rather than changing based on torch.rand stochasticity and changes in input. Running the model in torch displays expected output; for the same input, the output is different each time, and the output appears to loosely match the provided input phrase. After export to ONNX, the model's output stays constant regardless of input.
I suspect the forward method contains logic that doesn't translate well over to ONNX, although haven't located a specific cause yet.
Here's a notebook setup with the entire flow of the model here (including training) but I can simplify further if required. In the notebook, the codeblock at the very bottom will display the issue when re-ran multiple times and with different outputs. The exported ONNX always remains constant no matter what changes are made to the SAMPLE_TEXT while the torch output changes each time.

NOTE
The notebook is designed to run on mps. You'll need to modify device= in the Train the model section if running on a non-mps device.

https://gist.github.com/HudsonGraeme/e397068bec442fce0628efa0a3709303
Things I've tried:

Moving the model.eval() around within the export method
Removing model.eval() entirely
Adding torch.compile before exporting
Switching opset_versions between 11 and 16 (needed to modify the model slightly for versions below 14 due to flash attention using dot product operations)
Setting do_constant_folding to False in the ONNX export call
Removing the for loop from forward entirely, and generating only one character from the model
Removing the torch.rand call and replacing it with a constant float in the forward method

After this change the torch output stayed constant for a given input, but changed for different input as expected. The ONNX output still didn't change after modifying the input



Any help is appreciated!

The torch.special.exp2 function fails to compile when using the torch.compile optimized mode. However, the same code runs successfully in eager execution mode. I believe this discrepancy indicates a bug.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import traceback

def forward(x, device):

  
  x = torch.special.exp2(out = x, input = torch.rand([4, 2, 2, 8], dtype=torch.float32).to('cpu'))        
  return x
input_tensor = torch.rand([4, 2, 2, 8], dtype=torch.float32).to('cpu')

no_op_info = forward(input_tensor, 'cpu')
print("build succeded")

same_val = torch.allclose(no_op_info.to('cpu'),

nodes.title: Compilation Failure of torch.Var with out= argument in torch.compile Optimized Mode

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
The torch.cumsum function fails to compile when using the torch.compile optimized mode. However, the same code runs successfully in eager execution mode. I believe this discrepancy indicates a bug.
It appears that the decomposition for cumsum asserts that input tensors have the same device, while the eager op implementation does not have this requirement.
Same issue exists in #112495.
To reproduce
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import traceback

def forward(x, device):

  x = torch.cumsum(out=x, dim=0,input=torch.rand([10, 9, 8], dtype=torch.float32).to('cpu'))

  return x

input_tensor = torch.rand([10, 9, 8], dtype=torch.float32).to('cpu')
cuda_tensor = input_tensor.clone().to('cuda')
no_op_info = forward(input_tensor, 'cpu')
print("build succeded")
op_info = torch.compile(forward, mode='reduce-overhead',fullgraph=True,dynamic=True)(cuda_tensor, 'cuda')

same_val = torch.allclose(no_op_info.to('cpu'), 
                          op_info.to('cpu'), 
                          rtol=1e-3, atol=1e-3, 
                          equal_nan=True)
if same_val == False : 
      print("BUGBUG DIFFERENTIAL")
      raise ValueError('diff value')
else :
      print("no_error")

🐛 Describe the bug
Summary
Encountered a RuntimeError related to dynamic casting in the CPU loops of PyTorch.
Description
While running a specific operation in PyTorch, a RuntimeError was raised with the following message:
RuntimeError: !needs_dynamic_casting<func_t>::check(iter) INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "../aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/Loops.h":349, please report a bug to PyTorch.

This suggests an internal assertion failed within the native CPU loops of PyTorch.

import torch

In my model, there is layer like this,
A = SparseTensor(row=row, col=col, sparse_sizes=(m, self.num_nodes)).to_torch_sparse_coo_tensor()
Ax = mlp(A)
where mlp is nn.Linear layer
I'm trying to export above model to onnx. But I get an above issue "unsupported operator Error : aten ::sparse_coo_tensor".
My environment is
torch =2.0.0
cuda = 11.7
python=3.10
Alternatives
I'm trying to rewrite above code not usin sparse tensor.
But it takes a lot of memory. Or it takes a lot of time
Additional context
Is there any another option easier than writing custom onnx?

from mmdet.apis import train_detector

Here are some detailed information:

Everything was fine under PyTorch 1.8
The training was run inside docker container, with GPU of A100 × 4
By adding log in multiprocessing/reductions.py, I found that until the error message occured,  storage._share_fd_cpu() had been called over 60000+ times, and the accumulated storage.size() was about 37M.
By running ulimit -a I found the file descriptor limit was about 1M, and by running df /dev/shm I found the size of shared memory was about 100G.
By observing result shown in top command, I found the memory usage was no more than about 40% before the error occured.
The training dataset was composed by one set of data repeated 3 times. If I use only one copy, or just repeat a partial part, the error would not occur. I am not sure whether the error was caused by the size of the dataset or the data duplication. See the following image for details.

🐛 Describe the bug
import torch

torch.set_default_device('cuda')

@torch.compile
def f(x, y):
    return x.t() + y

f(torch.randn(2**25, 128), torch.randn(128, 2**25))
The concrete issue is that this results in us potentially choosing a config like XBLOCK=256, YBLOCK=512, which requires too much shared memory.
The reason we end up in this situation is: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/_inductor/triton_heuristics.py#L810
Basically, because we are limited to launching 65536 blocks on the second/third dim, triton_config will elect to scale up YBLOCK until we "fit" within the limit.
In this case, we start with a config like XBLOCK=256, YBLOCK=32, but we end up scaling YBLOCK to 512.
Possible solutions are:

Stop launching 2d configs, and just flatten it down to one axis of threadblocks.
Choose the XBLOCK axis to be the "large" one.
Scale down XBLOCK if XBLOCK * RBLOCK is too large.

cc @ezyang @msaroufim @wconstab @bdhirsh @anijain2305 @zou3519 @voznesenskym @penguinwu @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @peterbell10 @ipiszy @yf225 @chenyang78 @kadeng @muchulee8 @aakhundov @ColinPeppler

nodes.bodyText:
from typing import Any, Callable

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.autograd import Variable
from torch.distributed.utils import _apply_to_tensors


def hook(*args, **kwargs):
    assert 0, "Hello world!"


def register_backward_hook(output: Any, hook: Callable):
    if not torch.is_grad_enabled():
        return output

    def _register_hook(tensor: torch.Tensor):
        if tensor.requires_grad:
            tensor.register_hook(
                lambda *args, **kwargs: Variable._execution_engine.queue_callback(hook)
            )
        return tensor

    return _apply_to_tensors(_register_hook, output)


model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(3, 3, device="cuda"), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(3, 3, device="cuda")
)
out = model(torch.randn(2, 3, device="cuda"))
register_backward_hook(out, hook)
out.sum().backward()

🐛 Describe the bug
In Hugging Face transformers for some model architectures the gradients of trained models are being set to None when one uses gradient checkpointing.
I am not sure if this is a bug, but I managed to reproduce the behaviour in the snippet below.
import torch

from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint

class DummyLayer(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear1 = torch.nn.Linear(4, 4)
        self.ln1 = torch.nn.LayerNorm(4)

        self.linear2 = torch.nn.Linear(4, 4)
        self.ln2 = torch.nn.LayerNorm(4)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.linear1(x)
        x = self.ln1(x)

        x = self.linear2(x)
        x = self.ln2(x)
        return x

class DummyModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.emb = torch.nn.Embedding(4, 4)
        self.layers = torch.nn.ModuleList([DummyLayer() for _ in range(2)])
        self.head = torch.nn.Linear(4, 4)

        self._gradient_checkpointing_func = checkpoint

    def custom(self, module):
        def custom_forward(*inputs):
            inputs = module(inputs[0])
            return inputs
        return custom_forward
    
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.emb(x)

        for layer in self.layers:
            x = self._gradient_checkpointing_func(self.custom(layer), x)

        return x

model = DummyModel().to(0)
model.train()

for p in model.parameters():
    p.requires_grad_(True)

assert model.training

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
dummy_input = torch.LongTensor([[0, 1, 0, 1]]).to(0)

model.train()
logits = model(dummy_input)
loss = logits.sum()

loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

for n, param in model.named_parameters():
    if param.grad is None:
        raise ValueError(f"Parameter {n} has no gradient!")
Note this happens also if one uses use_reentrant=False:
- self._gradient_checkpointing_func = checkpoint
+ self._gradient_checkpointing_func = functools.partial(checkpoint, use_reentrant=False)

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
I'm trying to train a ResNet-18 model on Tiny Imagenet. I made a custom class which inherits from the nn.Module class. I load the model from torch.hub.load():
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from torchvision.models import ResNet18_Weights

class TinyImagenetResnet18(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base_model=False):
        super(TinyImagenetResnet18, self).__init__()
        self.loaded_weights = ResNet18_Weights.DEFAULT
        model = torch.hub.load('pytorch/vision:v0.10.0', 'resnet18', weights=self.loaded_weights)
        list_of_model = list(model.children())
        self.Conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 64, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1), bias=False)
        self.batch_norm1 = list_of_model[1]
        self.block1 = list_of_model[4]
        self.block2 = list_of_model[5]
        self.block3 = list_of_model[6]
        self.block4 = list_of_model[7]
        self.avg_pooling1 = list_of_model[8]
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_features=512, out_features=200, bias=True)
I create the input and output layers as I want them. However, if I use 3 input channels in the first layer (self.Conv1), loading the model does not go properly and it gets stuck in a self referencing feedback loop. I don't know much about the inner workings but I looked at the output trace and it seemed to do the same thing over and over. When I change the input channels to '1', it loads fine and continues with the program. When I let it run with input channels set to 3, it ran for 4 hours before it was terminated by my alloted time slot. Running the program doesn't produce an error, but it does suppress any print statements, also the ones before trying to load the model or even before I import the files which hold the relevant class.
I'm using the computer cluster from my university to run my experiments, which is why I'm not using the up to date versions of everything.
When I run it on my local computer it runs fine, so I think it has something to do with the versions.
I added the output trace for what it's worth. I had to cut it down because it was too large, so I don't know if it contains any useful information.

import warnings
import torch
import torch.utils.cpp_extension

source = '''
at::Tensor foo(at::Tensor x, int error_type) {
    std::ostringstream err_stream;
    err_stream << "Error with "  << x.type();

    TORCH_WARN(err_stream.str());
    return x.cos();
}
'''

t = torch.rand(2).double()

warn_mod = torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline(name='warnmod',
                                                    cpp_sources=[source],
                                                    functions=['foo'],
                                                    with_pytorch_error_handling=True)

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("error")
    warn_mod.foo(t, 0)

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
I want use flash attention on the cpu to speed up my automatic speech recognition(ASR) model, which is transformer-based.
In practice, the audio length in a batch may be different, which corresponds to different sequence lengths. The general approach is to use a mask tensor to indicate the sequence length, and add the mask to the attenton score before calculating the softmax in SDPA. Here is a simple example:
def get_mask(self, lengths, dtype=torch.float32):
    # lengths: the seq's length, shape is [batch, ]
    max_seq_len = lengths.max().item()
    row_vector = torch.arange(0, max_seq_len, 1)
    matrix = torch.unsqueeze(lengths, dim=-1)
    mask = row_vector < matrix
    mask = mask.to(dtype)
    mask_4d = 1 - mask[:, None, None, :]
    mask_4d = mask_4d * torch.finfo(dtype).min
    return mask_4d, mask

lengths = [2, 3]  # batch size is 2, first seq length is 2, second is 3
mask_4d, mask = get_mask(lengths)
print(mask)
"""
[
    [1, 1, 0],
    [1, 1, 1],
]
"""

# Assume here is a sdpa block
# query, key, value are both [batch, num_heads, max_seq_len, head_dim]
q_h = query * head_dim ** (-0.5)
attention_scores = torch.matmul(q_h, key.transpose(-1, -2))
attention_scores = attention_scores + mask_4d
attention_probs = nn.functional.softmax(attention_scores, dim=-1)
context_layer = torch.matmul(attention_probs, value)
As the code shows, mask4d needs to be used before softmax to eliminate erroneous results.
For now, I can use torch._scaled_dot_product_attention_math for this, but torch._scaled_dot_product_flash_attention doesn't work, it doesn't provide an api for mask.
However, when I see flash_attention_kernel in FlashAttentionKernel.cpp, which is the kernel for cpu flash attention, it could support mask just simply modify the code.
Alternatives

🐛 Describe the bug
When sharing a cuda module between processes in WSL2, the module weights seem to be initialized to zero for newly created processes.
# debug.py script
import torch


def test(model):
    print(model.weight)  # Prints 0, should print -0.0075
    model.load_state_dict({"weight": torch.tensor([[1.0]]), "bias": torch.tensor([0.0])})
    print(model.weight)  # Prints 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    device = torch.device("cuda")
    model = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1).to(device)
    model.share_memory()
    print(model.weight)  # Prints -0.0075
    ctx = torch.multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")
    proc = ctx.Process(target=test, args=(model,))
    proc.start()  # See test(model)
    proc.join()
    print(model.weight)  # Prints 1, model is indeed shared across processes
Expected behaviour:
Linear layer weight is -0.0075 both in the main process and in the new process. After updating the weights, it is 1 in both processes.
Actual behaviour:
Linear layer weight is 0 in the new process immediately after sharing. Updating changes the weights in both processes, so the module still seems to be shared properly.
This is only an issue for cuda modules. If you change the device to "cpu", the above code works as expected. Surprisingly, the behaviour causes even more trouble in Docker. I have created a minimal example using docker compose.

version: "3.8"
services:
  debug_container:
    build:
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: 1
              capabilities: [ gpu ]

Dockerfile
FROM pytorch/pytorch:2.1.0-cuda12.1-cudnn8-runtime

COPY debug.py /home/debug.py

ENTRYPOINT ["python", "/home/debug.py"]

nodes.bodyText:
📚 The doc issue
If someone is trying to use the C++ library with the Apple M1/M2 Processor then they have to compile pytorch from the source and use arm64 as a target. This should be mentioned in the  Installing C++ Distributions of PyTorch.
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
A simple instruction for compiling can be added to the docs.
Something like:
git clone -b main --recurse-submodule https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch.git
mkdir pytorch-build-arm64
cd pytorch-build-arm64
cmake -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS:BOOL=ON -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=11.00 -DUSE_MKLDNN=OFF -DUSE_QNNPACK=OFF -DUSE_PYTORCH_QNNPACK=OFF -DBUILD_TEST=OFF -DUSE_NNPACK=OFF -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE:STRING=Release -DPYTHON_EXECUTABLE:PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin/python3 -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX:PATH=../pytorch-install ../pytorch
cmake --build . --target install
NOTE: change the paths according to your system, i am using the python installed by homebrew. You will also need to install the required dependencies like PyYAML and typing-extensions.
This will build pytorch for the arm64 platform. It will also create another directory in the base folder called pytorch-install
Now, in your example-app you have to link to the pytorch-install dir
cmake -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/Path/to/this/folder/pytorch-install/...
cc @seemethere @malfet @osalpekar @atalman @svekars @carljparker @jbschlosser @albanD @snadampal
